lines.text: In 2020 NVIDIA noticed something. Deep learning did not need FP32's precision, but it did need FP32's range.
So they made a new sixteen-bit format that keeps the range and throws away the precision.
FP16 has five exponent bits and ten mantissa bits. BF16 has eight and seven.
Same sixteen bits. A completely different number.
The range is what a training run needs. Gradients get tiny. Activations get huge. Neither is a problem if the exponent can reach.
The precision is what inference likes. A weight at BF16 has fewer significant digits than one at FP16.
Which is why BF16 is the training format and FP16 is still the inference format.
And why both are everywhere: BF16 where the range matters, FP16 where the precision does.
The interesting part is what the throwaway bits buy. BF16 keeps the exponent identical to FP32.
Which means a BF16 number and an FP32 number have exactly the same exponent range.
You can convert between them by shifting bits. No rounding, no range check.
FP16 needs a clamp, because its exponent cannot represent FP32's biggest and smallest values.
The most useful number format is the one that is boring to convert.
